title: Steering vectors and activation engineering
summary: How adding or erasing one direction in a transformer's residual stream changes behavior: difference-of-means vectors, layer and scale, directional ablation of refusal, side effects and evaluation.
outcomes: Compute a difference-of-means steering vector from contrast pairs and explain why averaging beats a single pair
Use cosine similarity and projection to measure how much of a concept an activation carries
Choose an injection layer, token positions and coefficient, judging scale against the residual stream norm
Apply directional ablation and weight orthogonalization and explain how they differ from subtracting a vector
Design an evaluation that measures both the target behavior and capability side effects on held-out data

lessons.title: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream

blocks.md:
Suppose you want a chat model to be less sycophantic, to talk more positively, or to refuse less often. The usual tools are **prompting** (cheap, but it uses context and the model may ignore it) and **fine-tuning** (reliable, but it needs labeled data, compute and a new set of weights for every behavior).

**Activation engineering** is a third option: leave the weights and the prompt alone, and edit the model's internal activations during the forward pass. Turner et al. coined the term and showed that a single added vector can shift the topic or sentiment of GPT-2-XL's output.

Recall the GPT you built. Each token position carries a vector of size $d_{\text{model}}$, the **residual stream**. Every block reads it and adds its result back:

$x_{l+1} = x_l + \text{attn}_l(x_l) + \text{mlp}_l(x_l)$ (simplified; the real block applies the MLP after the attention update).

Because the stream is a running sum, anything you add at layer $l$ is visible to every later layer and to the unembedding. That makes it a natural place to intervene.

blocks.caption: Activation addition: at layer l, add a fixed steering vector v scaled by a coefficient c to the residual stream. Positive c strengthens the property v encodes, negative c suppresses it.

blocks.md: Why would one fixed vector do anything sensible? The **linear representation hypothesis** says high-level concepts (sentiment, language, tense, whether a request is harmful) are encoded as directions in activation space. Park et al. formalize this and prove that a linear representation in the input space connects to model steering, while one in the output space connects to linear probing. If a concept is a direction, then moving the activation along that direction should change how much of the concept the model thinks is present.

**ActAdd** (Activation Addition, Turner et al.) is the simplest recipe. Pick a contrast pair of prompts, for example "Love" and "Hate". Run each through the model and record the residual stream $h_+^l$ and $h_-^l$ just before layer $l$. The steering vector is $c\,(h_+^l - h_-^l)$. While the model processes a user prompt, add it to the residual stream at the same layer, aligned to the first token positions, and let the forward pass continue.

No gradient step is involved and one pair of prompts is enough, so iterating is fast: the authors report finding most of their contrast pairs in minutes.

blocks.title: ActAdd: one contrast pair, one added vector

scenes.caption: Run the two contrast prompts through the frozen model and cache the residual stream just before layer l. Nothing is trained.
Subtract the two cached activations and scale by c. What the prompts share cancels; what differs (roughly, love versus hate) remains.
Now run the user's prompt. Its residual stream flows through the lower layers untouched.
At layer l the vector is added to the stream, and every later layer reads the shifted activation. The output drifts toward the positive side of the pair.

blocks.md: A steering vector edits **activations**, not weights and not the prompt. It is computed once, before inference, and the same vector is added on every forward pass while it is switched on.

blocks.prompt: Turner et al. also injected a random vector, scaled to the same per-position norm as their working Anger minus Calm vector at c = +1. Predict: does the random vector change the completions as much as the steering vector does?
blocks.reveal:
No. The random vector did not noticeably change the qualitative distribution of completions. Even a random vector with the norm of the c = +10 steering vector shifted the outputs but left them about as coherent as the unsteered model.

So the effect comes from the **direction**, not merely from pushing the activations by a large amount. A good steering experiment always includes this random-direction control.

blocks.question: Why can a vector added only at layer l change the model's next-token prediction?
options: Because the model recomputes all earlier layers after the addition
Because the residual stream is a running sum: later layers read the shifted stream and the unembedding reads its final value
Because the vector is also added to the weights of every later layer
It cannot; the vector must be added at the last layer to matter
blocks.explain: Each block adds its output to the stream it reads, so a vector added at layer l stays in the sum. Later attention and MLP layers read it and react to it, and the final stream is what the unembedding decodes. No weights change and earlier layers are not rerun.

blocks.question: What does ActAdd need in order to build a steering vector?
options: A labeled dataset of a few thousand examples and a few gradient steps
A trained linear probe on the target concept
One pair of contrasting prompts and two forward passes
Access to the model's training data
blocks.explain: ActAdd is optimization-free: two forward passes on a prompt pair such as Love and Hate, a subtraction, and a scale factor. CAA, ITI (developed independently of ActAdd, slightly earlier) and RepE's reading vectors use more examples to get a cleaner direction; none of these fine-tunes the model.

lessons.title: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs

blocks.md:
A single prompt pair is noisy. "Love" minus "Hate" captures sentiment, but also whatever else happens to differ between those two token sequences. **Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA)** by Panickssery (published as Rimsky) et al. fixes this by averaging over many pairs.

Each CAA pair is the same multiple-choice question with an answer letter appended. The positive prompt ends with the letter that shows the behavior (for example the sycophantic answer), the negative prompt ends with the other letter. The activation is read at the answer-letter position, so the two prompts in a pair differ by a single token.

blocks.caption: The mean-difference (MD) vector at layer L. By linearity, the average of the pair differences equals the difference of the two class means.

blocks.md: Let us build one by hand. Take a toy residual stream with $d_{\text{model}} = 6$ and four pairs. Each pair shares a content vector; the positive member adds a hidden concept direction $(1, 0, 0.5, 0, 0, -0.5)$, the negative member subtracts it, and each activation also carries a little unrelated noise. (Simplified: real activations have thousands of dimensions and we would not know the true direction.)

blocks.title: Toy residual activations at the answer token

scenes.caption: Eight cached activations: four positive (P) and four negative (N). Row Pi and row Ni come from the same question with a different answer letter.
Dimension d0 already separates the classes: every P row is at least 0.5 there and every N row is 0 or below. But single dimensions can mislead; the concept is spread over d0, d2 and d5.
d5 points the other way: N rows sit higher. A good direction must combine dimensions with the right signs, which is exactly what subtracting the means does.

blocks.title: Difference of means, step by step

scenes.caption: Average the four positive rows column by column.
Average the four negative rows the same way.
Subtract. Content shared within each pair cancels, and much of the noise averages out. The result has length |v| = 2.368.
Divide by the length to get the unit direction used for measuring and ablating. Its cosine similarity with the hidden concept direction is 0.991.

blocks.md:
Two measurements appear everywhere in this field. The **cosine similarity** $\cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}$ compares directions and ignores length. The **projection** $a \cdot \hat v$ (with $\hat v = v/\|v\|$) says how far along the direction an activation sits, in the same units as the residual stream.

Projecting our eight activations onto $\hat v$ gives a one-number concept score for each. CAA uses the same idea to visualize which tokens in a real response align with a steering vector.

blocks.title: Projection of each activation onto the direction

scenes.caption: Onto the mean-difference direction: positives score 0.528 to 1.979, negatives score -1.531 to -0.475. A threshold at the midpoint of the class means (0.142) separates all eight.
Onto the direction from pair 4 alone (an ActAdd-style single pair): N1 now scores only -0.109, almost on the boundary. One pair's noise is baked into the direction.

blocks.title: Cosine with the hidden concept direction

scenes.caption: Each single-pair difference points roughly the right way, with cosines from 0.891 to 0.968 to the true direction.
The mean difference reaches 0.991, better than every individual pair. With hundreds of pairs, as in CAA, the gain is larger.

blocks.md:
Other methods extract the direction differently:

- **RepE** (Zou et al.) runs PCA (principal component analysis, which finds the direction of largest variance) on differences of activation pairs and calls the first principal component the *reading vector*; they report 5 to 128 stimuli is typically enough.
- **ITI** (Li et al.) works per attention head: it trains a linear probe on each head, keeps the top K heads by probe accuracy, and shifts each along a truthful direction by $\alpha$ times the activations' standard deviation along it.
- **Arditi et al.** take the difference of means between harmful and harmless instructions to find a refusal direction (lesson 4).

The best direction to **classify** with is not always the best direction to **steer** with. ITI compared both on LLaMA-7B: shifting along the probe's weight vector scored 34.8% true-and-informative on TruthfulQA, while shifting along the mass mean shift (difference of means) scored 42.3%. A probe can lean on any feature that happens to separate the classes, causal or not.

blocks.title: ITI on LLaMA-7B: which direction to shift along

scenes.caption: TruthfulQA true-times-informative score, each direction with its own best strength (2-fold cross-validation). The difference-of-means direction wins clearly; a random direction barely moves the score.

blocks.question: You build a CAA vector from 300 pairs where every positive prompt happens to be longer than its negative partner. What is the most likely problem?
options: None: averaging over 300 pairs removes all confounds
The vector partly encodes prompt length, because that difference is consistent across pairs and does not average out
The vector will have length zero
Mean difference only works with exactly one pair
blocks.explain: Averaging cancels differences that vary randomly across pairs. A difference that is the same in every pair, such as length, survives averaging and becomes part of the vector. CAA avoids this by making each pair identical except for one answer letter.

blocks.question: In the toy example, the single-pair direction from pair 4 still classifies all eight activations correctly. Why prefer the mean difference anyway?
options: It is the only direction with unit length
It makes projections of negatives exactly zero
Single-pair vectors cannot be added to the residual stream
It is closer to the true concept direction (cosine 0.991 vs 0.891), so steering along it changes less of everything else
blocks.explain: Classification only needs the right sign. Steering adds the whole vector, including its off-concept components. Pair 4's direction has a larger share of noise, so adding it would also push unrelated dimensions. The averaged vector is cleaner.

lessons.title: Where to add it, at which tokens, and how hard

blocks.md: A steering vector has three knobs: the **layer** where it is added, the **token positions** it is added to, and the **coefficient** $c$. None of them has a universal default, so every paper in this course sweeps them on held-out data.

**Layer.** Too early and the concept may not exist yet as a direction; too late and few layers remain to act on it. CAA found that behavioral clustering of the A/B activations emerges about one third of the way through Llama 2 Chat's layers, and their layer sweep peaked at layer 13 and its neighbors in the 7B model and at 14 or 15 in the 13B model.

ActAdd likewise found middle layers most effective, with the best layer depending on how abstract the concept is: the Love vector worked best at layer 6 of GPT-2-XL, the more abstract Conspiracy vector at layer 23.

scenes.caption: Simplified picture of a layer sweep: build a vector at each layer, add it at that layer, and score the behavior on held-out prompts.
Early injection: CAA's PCA plots show A/B activations separating by behavior only after a certain depth (for refusal in Llama 2 7B Chat, the clustering appears suddenly at layer 10).
Middle injection gives the largest effect in CAA's sweeps (layer 13 in the 7B model). ActAdd's wedding vector already works at the first layer of GPT-2-XL, peaks at layer 6, then declines.
Late injection is close to editing output tokens directly. Arditi et al. excluded layers beyond 0.8L so a refusal direction could not simply be the unembedding of words like I.

blocks.md:
**Positions.** ActAdd's vector is itself a short sequence of activations, aligned with the start of the user's prompt; the authors note that modifying the very last residual stream position reliably broke syntax. CAA adds its vector at every token position after the user's prompt, so each generated token is steered. Arditi et al. add their refusal vector at one layer but at all positions.

**Coefficient.** What matters is the vector's size *relative* to the residual stream it joins. Watch what adding $c\,v$ does to the held-out toy activation $x = (0.5, 1, 0, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5)$, which has $\|x\| = 1.414$ and projection $x \cdot \hat v = 0.686$.

blocks.tex: \cos(x + c\,v,\; v) = \frac{p + c\|v\|}{\sqrt{\|x\|^2 - p^2 + (p + c\|v\|)^2}}, \qquad p = x\cdot \hat v
blocks.caption: The part of x orthogonal to v is untouched; only the component along v grows. As c grows the steered vector points almost entirely along v.

blocks.title: How fast the steering vector takes over the stream

curves.label: share of squared norm along v

scenes.caption: Toy numbers: at c = 1 the steered vector already has cosine 0.927 with v, and at c = 4 it is 0.993. Simplified: real models also normalize the stream and react nonlinearly.
Make the stream ten times longer (norm 14.1), as at a deeper layer where residual norms are larger. The same c now barely moves the direction: scale has to be judged against the local norm.
Back to the toy stream. Past a point the original content is a rounding error; this is where generations lose coherence.
show: share of squared norm along v

blocks.md: Real models show the same picture. In ActAdd, the Anger minus Calm vector was effective at $c = +10$, which made the intervention nearly ten times the norm of the ordinary forward pass; the authors' rough reading is that about 90% of the stream is then the steering vector. They also note that intervention strengths are typically below 15 in magnitude. CAA reports that larger multipliers degraded open-ended text, as judged by GPT-4 and by human readers, so they limited the range.

blocks.prompt: ActAdd measured that residual-stream norms are much smaller in early layers than in later ones. Predict: if you take a vector extracted at layer 2 and add it, unchanged, at layer 20, will its effect be stronger or weaker than adding it at layer 2?
blocks.reveal: Weaker, all else equal. The vector's norm stays the same but the stream it joins at layer 20 is much longer, so its share of the stream shrinks, exactly like the second plot scene. ActAdd tried this transplant: completions became noticeably angrier, but less so than with the vector extracted at layer 20 itself (the authors also credit the gap to work done by layers 0 and 1). The practical rule: add a vector at the layer it was extracted from, or rescale it to the local norm.

blocks.md:
**Feature steering with sparse autoencoders.** Templeton et al. trained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on the middle-layer residual stream of Claude 3 Sonnet, giving millions of interpretable feature directions. To steer, they split the stream into SAE reconstruction plus error, clamp one feature to a chosen value, keep the error term, and apply this at every token position.

Clamping the Golden Gate Bridge feature to 10 times its maximum observed activation made the model self-identify as the bridge; Anthropic ran this as the public Golden Gate Claude demo for 24 hours in May 2024. Interesting effects typically needed values outside the observed range, and extreme clamps (around 100 times) produced nonsense.

blocks.title: Steering and ablation hooks in PyTorch
blocks.code:
# helper (not shown): acts() runs the model, caches resid at layer L
pos = acts(model, pos_prompts, layer=L)   # [n, d_model]
neg = acts(model, neg_prompts, layer=L)   # [n, d_model]

v = pos.mean(0) - neg.mean(0)             # difference of means
v_hat = v / v.norm()

def add_hook(module, args, output):
    h = output[0] if isinstance(output, tuple) else output
    h += c * v                            # every position
    return output

def ablate_hook(module, args, output):
    h = output[0] if isinstance(output, tuple) else output
    h -= (h @ v_hat).unsqueeze(-1) * v_hat
    return output

layer = model.model.layers[L]
handle = layer.register_forward_hook(add_hook)
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=60)
handle.remove()

scenes.caption: Cache residual activations at layer L for the positive and negative prompts (here the four toy pairs).
Difference of means and its unit vector, exactly the toy numbers from lesson 2.
The addition hook edits the layer's output in place. Simplified: it steers every position, while CAA adds only from the end of the prompt onward.
The ablation hook removes each position's component along v_hat (lesson 4). Its projection becomes 0 whatever it was.
Register the hook on decoder layer L, generate, then remove it so later calls run the unmodified model.

blocks.question: A vector extracted at layer 6 of a 48-layer model works well at c = 4. A colleague adds the same vector at layer 40 with c = 4 and sees almost no effect. What is the most likely explanation?
options: At layer 40 the residual stream is much larger, so the same c is a much smaller relative push, and the concept may be represented differently there
Steering vectors only work in the first half of a network
Adding at a later layer reverses the sign of the vector
The model detects the vector and removes it
blocks.explain: Residual norms grow with depth, so a fixed-size vector becomes relatively small; on top of that, a direction found at layer 6 need not be the direction the concept uses at layer 40. Extract and inject at the same layer, and sweep c relative to the local norm.

blocks.question: Why do Golden Gate style feature clamps need values far above the feature's observed maximum?
options: Because the SAE decoder vectors have zero norm
The authors suspect the single clamped feature is normally co-active with several related features, so it must be pushed harder on its own
Because clamping only works at the last token
Because the error term cancels the clamp
blocks.explain: Templeton et al. suggest that in natural text a feature fires together with correlated features of related meaning. Steering one of them alone needs a stronger push to produce the same downstream effect. Push too far (around 100 times) and the model devolves into nonsense.

lessons.title: Directional ablation: erasing refusal from the residual stream

blocks.md: Adding a vector pushes every activation by the same amount. Sometimes you want something else: remove a concept entirely, however much of it each activation contains. Arditi et al. did this for **refusal**. Across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters they found a single direction such that erasing it stops the model refusing harmful requests, while adding it makes the model refuse even harmless ones.

They built the direction with the same difference of means as lesson 2. The training sets are 128 harmful instructions (from AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct and TDC2023) and 128 harmless ones (from Alpaca); separate 32-instruction validation sets (harmful ones from HarmBench) are kept for choosing the direction. Activations are read at the **post-instruction** tokens, the chat-template tokens after the user's message, where the model is about to decide how to answer. Each position $i$ and layer $l$ gives a candidate $r_i^{(l)}$, so there are (number of positions) x (number of layers) candidates to choose from.

blocks.caption: Directional ablation: subtract the component of x along the unit direction r-hat. Applied at every layer and every token position.

blocks.title: Ablating and adding the direction in the toy stream

scenes.caption: Reuse the toy direction as r-hat and take the positive activation P2. Its projection is r-hat dot x = 1.583: plenty of the concept is present.
Subtract 1.583 times r-hat. Every coordinate changes a little, and the projection of x' onto r-hat is now exactly 0. Its norm drops from 2.179 to 1.498.
Ablation is not subtraction of a fixed amount. The negative activation N1 had projection -0.475; ablation moves it up to 0 too. Harmless activations change, which is why harmless KL is checked.

The opposite move: add v (length 2.368) to the negative N3. Its projection goes from -1.346 to 1.023, past the positive class's 0.528 minimum. This is how adding the refusal direction induces refusal.

blocks.prompt: Arditi et al. ablate the direction at every layer, not just the one it was extracted from. Predict why ablating at a single layer might not be enough.
blocks.reveal: Later attention and MLP layers can write the direction back into the stream. Erasing it at layer $l$ removes what is present at $l$, but a later block that reads other features (the harmful content itself is still in the stream) may recompute it. Ablating at every layer and position, or equivalently making every writer unable to write it, closes that gap. Addition, by contrast, only needs one layer: the added vector persists in the running sum.

blocks.md: **Weight orthogonalization.** The same ablation can be baked into the weights. Every matrix that writes to the residual stream (token embedding, positional embedding, attention output, MLP output, plus their output biases) gets its column vectors projected away from $\hat r$. Then no component can ever write along $\hat r$, and the edited model behaves like the ablated one with no runtime hooks. Arditi et al. show the two are equivalent and present this as a white-box jailbreak.

scenes.caption: A toy 6 x 3 output projection W. Its columns have projections 0.844, 0 and 0.607 onto r-hat, so inputs to columns 0 and 2 write along the refusal direction.
After W' = W - r-hat r-hat-transpose W, every column has projection 0. Column 1 was already orthogonal and is unchanged. For z = (1, 0.5, -1), W'z equals the ablation of Wz exactly.

blocks.md: How was one direction picked from all the candidates? Each is scored on separate validation sets: how much ablating it reduces refusal on harmful prompts (bypass score), whether adding it induces refusal on harmless prompts, and the KL divergence it causes on harmless prompts when ablated. The chosen direction minimizes the bypass score subject to: induce score above 0, KL below 0.1, and layer below 0.8L, where L is the number of layers. Refusal is then judged on JailbreakBench's 100 harmful instructions in two ways: a **refusal score** (does the reply contain a stock phrase such as "I'm sorry" or "As an AI") and a **safety score** (does Llama Guard 2 rate the reply safe).

scenes.caption: Every post-instruction position and every layer yields a candidate vector from the training split.
Filters on a separate validation split: it must induce refusal when added, must barely change harmless behavior when ablated, and must not sit next to the unembedding.
Among survivors, keep the one whose ablation most reduces refusal. The evaluation sets are kept disjoint from both splits.

blocks.md: This is dual use. Removing a single direction strips the safety behavior from an open-weights chat model with minimal effect on other capabilities, which the authors read as evidence that current safety fine-tuning is brittle. They also show that adversarial suffixes work partly by suppressing this same direction.

blocks.question: You want to stop refusals. Option A subtracts the refusal vector (x minus r) at one layer. Option B ablates r-hat at every layer. Arditi et al. found both bypass refusal comparably. What is B's advantage on harmless prompts?
options: B is faster at inference
B also improves MMLU
A shifts every activation by a fixed amount, pushing harmless ones far past zero; B only removes what is there, so it raised loss on harmless data less
There is no difference on harmless prompts
blocks.explain: Subtraction moves all activations by the same vector, so prompts with little refusal content end up strongly negative along r, an unnatural state. Ablation sets the component to zero regardless. In the paper's comparison, activation addition in the negative direction caused higher loss on harmless data than directional ablation.

blocks.question: Which edit makes a model unable to write the refusal direction, permanently and without inference-time hooks?
options: Orthogonalize the output matrices that write to the residual stream (embeddings, attention out, MLP out, and their biases) against r-hat
Orthogonalize only the final unembedding matrix
Add r to the bias of the last layer
Set the layer norm gains to zero
blocks.explain: Only those matrices write into the residual stream. Projecting r-hat out of each of them means no component can ever contribute along r-hat, which is equivalent to directional ablation at every layer and position. Editing only the unembedding would change which tokens are read out, not the internal direction.

lessons.title: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector

blocks.md: A steering result has two halves. Did the **target behavior** move, on prompts not used to build the vector? And what **else** moved: general knowledge, fluency, behavior on unrelated prompts? Good papers report both, and the tradeoff between them sets the usable coefficient.

blocks.title: CAA on top of system prompts (Llama 2 13B Chat, corrigibility)

scenes.caption: Average probability of the corrigible answer on held-out A/B questions, steering at layer 13 with no system prompt. Steering moves it from 0.57 down to 0.45 or up to 0.83.
With a system prompt asking for the behavior, the baseline rises to 0.79, and adding the vector still pushes it to 0.93.
With a system prompt asking for the opposite, steering still shifts it from 0.53 to 0.59 or 0.32. Steering composes with prompting rather than replacing it.

blocks.md: Capability side effects in CAA were small on a multiple-choice proxy: on MMLU (10 questions from each of 57 subjects, reformatted as A/B), the unsteered 13B model put 0.63 average probability on the correct answer, and steering with multiplier +1 or -1 at layer 14 kept it between 0.57 and 0.65 across all seven behaviors. Open-ended text was more sensitive: larger multipliers degraded quality, which is why the paper limits the range.

blocks.title: CAA side effect on MMLU (Llama 2 13B Chat, layer 14)

scenes.caption: Unsteered: average probability 0.63 on the correct MMLU answer.
Multiplier +1: 0.59 to 0.65. The largest drop is from adding the refusal vector (0.59).
Multiplier -1: 0.57 to 0.64. Subtracting the hallucination vector costs the most here (0.57).

blocks.md: ITI shows the tradeoff sharply. On the instruction-tuned Alpaca, ITI raised TruthfulQA true-times-informative from 32.5% to 65.1%. The same intervention raised cross-entropy on pretraining text from 2.56 to 2.92 and produced a next-token KL divergence of 0.61 from the unsteered model. As the strength $\alpha$ grows, the true-times-informative score traces an upside-down U: past the peak, answers become truthful by saying less, and helpfulness falls.

blocks.title: ITI on Alpaca: TruthfulQA before and after

scenes.caption: Alpaca without intervention, 2-fold cross-validation so no question used to find directions is scored.
With ITI, true-times-informative roughly doubles. The price is visible elsewhere: cross-entropy 2.56 to 2.92 and KL 0.61 against the original model.

blocks.md: For the refusal ablation, Arditi et al. ran MMLU, ARC, GSM8K and TruthfulQA (plus WinoGrande and TinyHellaSwag in the appendix). Except for Qwen 7B and Yi 34B, all scores of the orthogonalized models stayed within 99% confidence intervals of the originals, but TruthfulQA accuracy dropped consistently, plausibly because its misinformation and conspiracy questions sit close to refusal territory. ActAdd checked factual recall on ConceptNet (LAMA) and found negligible change in the probability of the correct answer.

Evaluate a steering vector like a model change:

1. Build the vector on one split, choose layer and c on a second, report on a third.
2. Measure the target behavior directly (A/B probability, refusal substrings plus a safety classifier, an LLM judge checked against human ratings).
3. Measure collateral damage: a capability benchmark, loss on ordinary text, KL on unrelated prompts, and read generations.
4. Compare with a random direction of equal norm, a system prompt and fine-tuning.

LLM judges are convenient but not neutral. CAA used GPT-4 to score open-ended answers from 1 to 10 and notes the scores are sensitive to the rubric's wording; they spot-checked against their own ratings. String-matching refusal detectors have the opposite problem: they catch "I'm sorry" but not a harmful reply, so Arditi et al. paired them with Llama Guard 2.

Finally, the geometry itself is an assumption. Park et al. point out that cosine similarity and projection depend on the inner product, and the Euclidean one is not guaranteed to respect the model's semantics. They derive a *causal inner product*, $\langle a, b\rangle_C = a^{\top}\mathrm{Cov}(\gamma)^{-1} b$ with $\gamma$ the unembedding vectors, under which causally separable concepts are orthogonal. Practically: if a concept is not represented linearly, or two concepts share a direction, a steering vector will drag both along, and only careful side-effect evaluation will show it.

blocks.question: A team builds a sycophancy vector from 500 A/B pairs, picks the layer and coefficient that maximize the score on those same 500 pairs, and reports a large effect. What is the main flaw?
options: They should have used fewer pairs
Sycophancy cannot be represented linearly
They should have reported MMLU instead of the behavior score
The vector, the hyperparameters and the reported score all come from the same data, so the effect is likely overstated; it needs held-out validation and test splits
blocks.explain: Choosing layer and c on the evaluation data overfits them to it. CAA scores on 50 held-out questions, ITI uses 2-fold cross-validation, and Arditi et al. keep train, validation and evaluation sets pairwise disjoint. Capability checks are needed too, but they do not fix the leak.

blocks.question: Your refusal-steered model keeps its MMLU score, yet users report rambling, repetitive answers. Which check would have caught this?
options: Raising the coefficient
Measuring loss or KL on ordinary prompts and reading open-ended generations, not just multiple-choice accuracy
Running MMLU with more subjects
Using a single contrast pair instead of many
blocks.explain: MMLU in the A/B format reads one token's probability, which can survive while generation quality collapses. CAA saw exactly this: multiple-choice capability held while larger multipliers degraded open-ended text. Loss on ordinary text, KL on unrelated prompts and reading samples catch it.

blocks.question: Why is a random vector of the same norm a necessary baseline?
options: To check the hook is installed
Because random vectors are always better at steering
To show the effect comes from the direction and not from merely perturbing the stream by that much
To estimate the residual stream norm
